cleanIntro: The BL-22 is a short-throw lever-action rimfire with an exposed hammer and no separate manual safety — the hammer's three positions ARE the safety system, and Browning's handling doctrine for this rifle is built around keeping it at half-cock. Every maintenance session therefore starts and ends with hammer discipline, not a safety button. The rifle publishes no disassembly at any level: the action is cleaned open through the ejection port, the bore from the muzzle, and the tubular magazine under the barrel comes out as an assembled unit for unloading. This guide walks exactly that — the two unloading routes, the thumb-cushioned hammer lowering that is this rifle's one genuinely practiced skill, the three prohibitions the book states, and the assembled-rifle cleaning routine.

steps.title: Know the rifle you are holding: no safety button anywhere on it
steps.action: The BL-22 has no separate manual safety to find, and looking for one teaches you the wrong lesson about the rifle. What it has instead is an exposed hammer with three positions — full-cock, half-cock, and dropped — plus a built-in interlock that keeps it from firing until the finger lever and breech bolt are fully closed. The hammer is your status indicator: read its position every time the rifle comes into your hands, the way you would check a safety lever on anything else.
steps.prose: Half-cock, chamber empty, is the resting state this whole guide works from and returns to.
steps.quote: Like many lever-action rifles with an exposed hammer, the BL-22 does not have a separate manual “safety.”
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Operation of the Hammer
steps.warn: There is no safety button. The hammer position is the status indicator.

steps.title: Lower the hammer with your thumb in the V — the one skill this rifle demands
steps.action: Moving the hammer from full-cock to half-cock requires briefly depressing the trigger to start the hammer forward, and while the trigger is depressed the half-cock notch cannot catch a slipped hammer — which is why Browning's procedure cushions it: place the end of your thumb in the V space between the hammer and the firing pin, squeeze the trigger to release the hammer onto your thumb, take your finger OFF the trigger, then ease the hammer down to half-cock. With a scope mounted, the thumb goes in from the side. Practice this with the rifle verified empty until it is smooth.
steps.prose: Finger off the trigger before the hammer moves is the load-bearing detail — with the trigger released, the half-cock notch is live again and will catch a slip.
steps.quote: 1. Place the end of the thumb in the "V" space between the hammer and the firing pin so that it can act as a cushion against accidental hammer fall (Figure 6).
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Operation of the Hammer > LOWERING THE HAMMER
steps.warn: While the trigger is depressed, the half-cock notch will NOT catch a slipped hammer. Thumb in the V first.

steps.title: Never fit a hammer extension to a BL-22
steps.action: Do not install a hammer extension or hammer spur on this rifle, whatever a scope's clearance seems to argue. Browning prohibits it outright: an extension can cause a malfunction and create a hazardous condition — on a rifle whose entire safety system runs through controlled thumb pressure on the hammer, anything that changes the hammer's geometry changes the one procedure that must never slip. The manual's own answer to scope clearance is different: insert the tip of the thumb from the side.
steps.prose: Aftermarket hammer spurs are sold specifically for scoped lever guns, which is exactly why the prohibition is printed rather than assumed.
steps.quote: WARNING: NEVER USE A HAMMER EXTENSION (HAMMER SPUR) ON YOUR BL-22. USING A HAMMER EXTENSION CAN RESULT IN A MALFUNCTION AND POSSIBLY CREATE A HAZARDOUS CONDITION.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Operation of the Hammer > LOWERING THE HAMMER
steps.warn: No hammer extensions, ever. Scope clearance is handled with the thumb from the side.

steps.title: Unload with the lever — and keep cycling after the last round
steps.action: With the muzzle safe and fingers off the trigger, cycle the finger lever fully down and fully closed, repeatedly, ejecting each cartridge until nothing more comes out — and then keep working the lever several times more. The tube magazine feeds as long as it holds anything, so the stop condition is not 'no round ejected this cycle', it is a visual check: hold the action open and look into the chamber and the magazine until you can see both are empty. Catch the ejected rounds rather than letting rimfire cartridges bounce off the floor.
steps.prose: Only when the rifle is proved empty does the lever close and the hammer come down — using the thumb-in-the-V procedure, every time.
steps.quote: WARNING: ALWAYS WORK THE LEVER SEVERAL TIMES AFTER THE LAST UNFIRED CARTRIDGE HAS BEEN EJECTED TO MAKE SURE NO CARTRIDGES REMAIN IN THE CHAMBER OR MAGAZINE. VISUALLY CHECK, HOLDING THE ACTION OPEN, TO MAKE SURE THE CHAMBER IS EMPTY AND THAT THERE ARE NO CARTRIDGES IN THE MAGAZINE.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Unloading > UNLOADING THE RIFLE USING THE LEVER

steps.title: Or unload from the magazine tube — and mind the round it will not give up
steps.action: The faster route pulls the ammunition out at the source: cycle the lever fully down to clear the chamber and keep the bolt open, pull the inner magazine assembly completely out of the outer tube, lower the muzzle and let the cartridges slide out into your hand. Then the trap this method sets: the last cartridge does not slide out of the magazine — it is held in position for chambering. Reinsert the empty magazine assembly, swing the lever up to chamber that last round, then fully down to eject it. Finish with the same several-extra-cycles and visual check as the lever method.
steps.prose: The held-back last round is the reason this method has a warning printed in the middle of it. Count what came out of the tube against what went in if you can.
steps.quote: WARNING: THE LAST CARTRIDGE IN THE MAGAZINE WILL NOT SLIDE OUT OF THE MAGAZINE, BUT WILL BE HELD IN POSITION FOR CHAMBERING. BE SURE TO UNLOAD THIS LAST CARTRIDGE BY CYCLING THE BOLT WITH THE FINGER LEVER.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Unloading > UNLOADING FROM THE MAGAZINE
steps.warn: The tube retains its last cartridge. It must be chambered and ejected with the lever.

steps.title: Three rimfire lengths are legal in this one — read the barrel anyway
steps.action: Unlike most of its rimfire siblings, the BL-22 digests 22 Short, 22 Long and 22 Long Rifle, in any combination, as designated on the barrel — the magazine holds 15 Long Rifle, 17 Long, or 22 Short cartridges. A lever gun does not care about cycling impulse the way an autoloader does, which is what makes the mixed diet possible. The rule that survives is the same as everywhere else: only what is inscribed on the right side of the barrel, and examine every cartridge you load.
steps.prose: Mixed lengths in the tube are fine; mixed calibres on the bench are not. Keep anything that is not .22 rimfire somewhere else.
steps.quote: The BL-22 must be used only with 22 rimfire ammunition as designated on the barrel (22 Short, Long or Long Rifle).
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Ammunition

steps.title: Never dry fire it, and never touch the trigger mechanism
steps.action: Two prohibitions bracket the fire-control group. Do not dry fire the BL-22 — a rimfire firing pin without a rim to strike lands on the chamber mouth, and Browning states it can render the firearm inoperable. And make no attempt to alter the two-stage trigger's pull: it is pre-set at the factory, and tampering may damage it beyond repair — beyond repair meaning a new trigger mechanism, not an adjustment visit. When the hammer needs to come down, it comes down on your thumb via the lowering procedure, never by snapping on an empty chamber.
steps.prose: The dry-fire notice is printed twice, once in the general description and once under its own heading. The trigger notice stands alone under Trigger Adjustment, which is a heading with no adjustment in it.
steps.quote: NOTICE: NO ATTEMPT SHOULD EVER BE MADE TO ALTER THE TRIGGER PULL. ANY ATTEMPT TO TAMPER WITH THE TRIGGER MAY DAMAGE IT BEYOND REPAIR.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Trigger Adjustment (dry fire: General Description and Operation, repeated under Dry Firing)
steps.warn: No dry firing. No trigger work. Both are stated as damage, not as preference.

steps.title: Browning publishes no BL-22 disassembly — the action cleans open
steps.action: Stop looking for a takedown: there is none in this book. No lever removal, no bolt removal, no buttstock or trigger work — the closing notice bars going further than the manual explains, and the manual explains cleaning the assembled rifle only. Open the action with the finger lever; to give the cleaning gear room, it may be necessary to raise the lever about five degrees so the carrier drops below the chamber. That open action is your whole working access: chamber and bore ahead of it, receiver cavity around it.
steps.prose: A rifle with no published strip still has a published boundary, and this is it — anything deeper is a Browning service centre or the Arnold, Missouri facility.
steps.quote: 1. Open the action using the finger lever (Figure 12). To accommodate cleaning, it may be necessary to raise the lever about five degrees to lower the carrier below the chamber.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 1
steps.warn: Never take the rifle apart further than the manual explains. Deeper work goes to a gunsmith.

steps.title: Bore from the muzzle — buy the muzzle guard the manual asks for
steps.action: With the barrel fixed to the receiver, cleaning runs from the muzzle: rod with a slotted tip or jag, patch snug in the bore, in at the muzzle and back and forth several times. The crown is the exposure — every stroke passes the surface that decides accuracy, and Browning goes as far as recommending you purchase a muzzle guard to keep the rod off it. Powder fouling comes off with nitro solvent on a patch; heavy fouling takes a brass bore brush pushed completely through before it is withdrawn, so bristles do not fold and shed in the bore.
steps.prose: A normal amount of powder residue is expected and not serious — chase the fouling, not the discolouration.
steps.caution: Every stroke passes the crown. Guard it.
steps.quote: We recommend purchasing a muzzle guard to prevent the cleaning rod from striking the muzzle.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 2

steps.title: Dry the bore, oil it lightly, and prove nothing was left behind
steps.action: Wipe the chamber and bore dry once the fouling is gone, then pass one slightly oiled patch through for preservation — a fine, light gun oil, nothing heavier. Then the step that exists because people skip it: inspect the barrel and chamber to be certain no patch has been left in either, and remove any that remain. A forgotten patch is a bore obstruction, and the manual's own barrel-obstruction warning is what it turns into at the next range session.
steps.prose: Look from the muzzle with the action open against a light — on a lever gun that line of sight is available and free.
steps.quote: 5. Inspect the barrel and chamber to be certain no patches have inadvertently been left in them. Remove any that remain.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, steps 4-5

steps.title: Receiver brushed out, oil in films and never in pours
steps.action: Use a small brush or rag to lift dirt out of the receiver cavity and the reachable action parts, then lightly lubricate the moving parts with a high-quality light gun oil — sparingly, a very light film is sufficient. The pour-in temptation is specifically banned on this rifle for a wooden reason: oil poured into the receiver drains down into the stock wood, softens it permanently and loosens the stock. Finish by wiping every exposed metal surface with a lightly oiled cloth until the finger marks are gone; finger marks are where moisture starts.
steps.prose: Wood surfaces take a light gun oil or a quality furniture wax — one or the other, never both.
steps.caution: Oil migrates downhill into the stock. Films, not pours.
steps.quote: NOTICE: DO NOT POUR LARGE QUANTITIES OF OIL INTO THE RECEIVER OR OTHER PARTS. IT CAN DRAIN DOWN TO THE WOOD AND SOFTEN IT, CAUSING PERMANENT DAMAGE AND LOOSENING OF THE STOCK.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 6

steps.title: Sights and scope — 3/8-inch grooves, correct bases only
steps.action: The folding rear sight adjusts for elevation by loosening the two small locking screws in its face and sliding the U-notch plate — up to raise impact, down to lower it, one etched graduation moving impact about two inches at 50 yards. Windage is drift adjustment in the dovetails with a wood dowel or comparable nonmetallic punch: rear sight moves the way you want impact to move, front sight moves opposite. For glass, the receiver takes 3/8-inch groove or tip-off mounts, and Browning's notice is blunt — always use the correct bases for this rifle, or damage could occur.
steps.prose: Sight work happens on a rifle proved empty, hammer at half-cock, same as every other job in this guide.
steps.quote: NOTICE: ALWAYS USE THE CORRECT BASES FOR THIS RIFLE. DAMAGE COULD OCCUR TO THE RIFLE.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Mounting a Scope (elevation and windage: Sight Adjustment)

steps.title: Field strip complete — which on a BL-22 means the action open and nothing removed
steps.action: That is the entire published routine: rifle unloaded and proved by eye, action cleaned open, bore cleaned from the muzzle behind a guard, oil in light films, exterior wiped down. Nothing came off the rifle, so nothing goes back on — the finish of a BL-22 session is closing the lever, lowering the hammer to half-cock with your thumb in the V, and confirming the magazine tube is locked in place. Clean it after every day of shooting and more often if it gets excessively dirty; a minimum session is a wipe-down and oiling the key parts.
steps.prose: If a function problem survives a thorough cleaning, the next stop is a Browning Recommended Service Center or the Arnold, Missouri facility — not a deeper teardown at your bench.
steps.quote: Clean your firearm after every day of shooting, and more often if it becomes excessively dirty. A minimum cleaning includes wiping down the firearm and oiling key parts. Regular maintenance will also include cleaning the barrel.
steps.cite: Browning BL-22 Rimfire Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES

deepAbsentReason: The BL-22 Owner's Manual publishes NO disassembly of the rifle at any level — no bolt removal, no lever removal, no trigger-group access, no stock removal. Its entire maintenance content is performed on the assembled rifle with the action open via the finger lever (raised about five degrees to drop the carrier where needed): bore cleaned from the muzzle behind a recommended muzzle guard, receiver cavity brushed out, moving parts oiled in a light film, exterior wiped. The book's closing notice bars taking the firearm apart further than it explains and routes deeper service to a qualified gunsmith or Browning's Arnold, Missouri facility, and it separately prohibits any alteration of the factory-set two-stage trigger as damage beyond repair. There is therefore no deeper procedure to present, and none has been invented.

cleaning.name: BORE & CHAMBER (from the muzzle, action open)
tasks: Action open via the finger lever; lever raised ~5° if the carrier needs to sit below the chamber
Rod with slotted tip or jag, snug patch, entered at the muzzle — use a muzzle guard, per the manual's own recommendation
Nitro solvent patch for powder fouling; brass bore brush for heavy fouling, pushed fully through before withdrawing
Wipe dry, one slightly oiled patch for preservation
Inspect barrel and chamber for forgotten patches before closing the action

cleaning.name: RECEIVER & ACTION (assembled)
tasks: Small brush or rag for dirt inside the receiver and reachable action parts
Light film of quality light gun oil on moving parts — sparingly
Never pour oil into the receiver: it drains into the stock wood, softens it and loosens the stock

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR, WOOD & FINISHES
tasks: All exposed metal wiped with a lightly oiled cloth until finger marks are gone
Light oil film any time the rifle has seen weather or handling
Keep DEET repellents, sunscreen and strong chemicals off the finishes
Wood: light gun oil or quality furniture wax — not both

cleaning.name: SIGHTS
tasks: Elevation: two locking screws in the sight face loosened, U-notch plate moved (one graduation ≈ 2" at 50 yards), screws lightly retightened
Windage: drift in the dovetails with a wood or nonmetallic dowel — rear sight with the impact, front sight against it
Scope: 3/8" groove / tip-off mounts, correct BL-22 bases only

reassembly: Nothing was removed — the BL-22 cleans assembled, so this is a return-to-service check rather than a rebuild.
Confirm the bore is clear against a light and only a light oil film remains in the action.
Confirm the inner magazine assembly is fully inserted and locked in the outer tube.
Close the action by returning the finger lever fully up.
Lower the hammer to half-cock using the published procedure: thumb in the V between hammer and firing pin, squeeze the trigger to release, finger OFF the trigger, ease the hammer down.
Store chamber empty, hammer at half-cock — the manual's recommended carrying and storage state.
Never test the mechanical function with live ammunition, and never dry fire to prove the trigger.
fncheck: With the rifle proved empty, work the finger lever through its full short arc and feel it close completely — the interlock means an incompletely closed lever is a rifle that will not fire, so a lever that will not seat flush is a real finding, usually debris in the action. Confirm the hammer holds at half-cock against firm thumb pressure and that the trigger will not drop it from half-cock. Confirm the magazine assembly locks into the outer tube. Look through the bore from the muzzle against a light for patch material. Do NOT dry fire to test the trigger — lower the hammer onto your thumb per the published procedure instead — and never test function with live ammunition.
